title: CHAPTER 9: GREEN REVOLUTION, FOOD SECURITY AND SUSTAINABILITY

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The chapter explores the history, methods, and impact of the Green Revolution on food production.
Food security framework is analyzed under the Four Pillars of Food Security established by the FAO.
Sustainable Agriculture focuses on balancing agricultural yield with long-term ecological preservation.

blocks.content: The Green Revolution refers to the dramatic increase in agricultural production in India (and developing countries) during the 1960s–70s, primarily due to the introduction of high-yielding varieties (HYV) of wheat and rice, expanded irrigation, and increased use of fertilisers and pesticides.

cells: Mid 1960s to mid 1970s (first phase); ongoing improvements since
Dr. Norman Borlaug (CIMMYT) — Father of Green Revolution; Dr. M.S. Swaminathan — Father of Green Revolution in India
Lerma Rojo-64 and Sonora-64 from Mexico; hybridised with Indian varieties at IARI
Short straw; lodging-resistant; high harvest index; respond well to fertilisers
India went from food-deficient (ship-to-mouth) to food-surplus; self-sufficiency in cereals
Regional disparity; environmental degradation; water table depletion; soil health issues; not equitable
Diversification to pulses, oilseeds, horticulture; east India focus; climate-smart varieties
Bt cotton adoption; GM crops research; precise breeding technologies

blocks.content: Food security exists when all people at all times have physical, social and economic access to sufficient safe and nutritious food that meets their dietary needs and food preferences for an active and healthy life (FAO, 1996 World Food Summit definition).

items: Sufficient food production, imports, and reserves to meet needs: Availability
People have resources to obtain food (physical and economic access): Access
Proper use of food through clean water, sanitation, healthcare; nutritional security: Utilisation
Access to adequate food at all times; no disruption from climate, price shocks: Stability

cells: Distribute food at subsidised rates through ration shops (fair price shops)
Poorest of poor; 35 kg grain/family/month at Rs.2/kg wheat, Rs.3/kg rice
Legal right to food; 75% rural, 50% urban population covered; 5 kg/person/month
Hot cooked meal to school children; improve enrolment, retention, nutrition
Supplementary nutrition, immunisation, health check-up to children < 6 years
Free ration (5 kg grain) to NFSA beneficiaries during COVID; extended till Dec 2023

items: The Four Pillars of Food Security defined by the FAO are critical and frequently queried in competitive exams.
Exam questions often contrast high-yield Green Revolution practices with Sustainable Agriculture concepts.

blocks.content: Sustainable agriculture aims to meet current food needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It balances economic viability, environmental stewardship, and social equity.

items: Minimum soil disturbance + permanent soil cover + crop rotation; adopted globally: Conservation Agriculture (CA)
Sowing without ploughing; reduces fuel cost; maintains soil structure; Happy Seeder for wheat after paddy: Zero Tillage (No-Till)
Avoids synthetic chemicals; uses compost, FYM, biofertilisers; PKVY, PGS-India: Organic Farming
Zero Budget Natural Farming (ZBNF) — promoted by Subhash Palekar; uses cow dung/urine based preparations (Jeevamrit, Bijamrit): Natural Farming
Integration of trees with crops/livestock; improves biodiversity, carbon sequestration: Agroforestry
Adapts to climate change; drought-tolerant varieties; precision irrigation; carbon credits: Climate-Smart Agriculture
Use of GPS, sensors, drones, satellite imagery; variable rate application; IoT in farms: Precision Agriculture
